caption: The galaxy cluster Abell S1063, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows Abell S1063, a cluster of galaxies. A galaxy cluster is a huge gathering of galaxies bound together by gravity, and Hubble observed this one as part of its Frontier Fields programme.

The interest lies partly in what sits behind the cluster. A cluster holds an enormous amount of mass, and mass bends the path of light passing near it. Abell S1063 works like a natural lens. Light from galaxies lying much farther away is bent and enlarged on its way to us, and that boost makes them bright enough for Hubble to pick up.

Without the cluster acting as a magnifier, those faint and distant galaxies would stay out of reach. Programmes like Frontier Fields use this effect to study galaxies that would otherwise be too dim to see.
explore: Hubble observed the cluster with two cameras, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, through filters that run from blue visible light into the near-infrared. The cluster's distance is given as a redshift of 0.348 rather than in light-years.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is infrared, which the eye cannot see, and even the visible part is far too faint to see without a large telescope.

alt: A Hubble image of the galaxy cluster Abell S1063.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3169, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble catches the spiral galaxy NGC 3169 from a steep angle, so the viewer seems to be stretching up to peer over a wall toward the galaxy's bright centre. That wall is the thick dust woven through the galaxy's spiral arms.

Spiral galaxies are common sights, and what makes this one worth a second look is the viewpoint. Dust in space is a mixture of many kinds of particles, among them water ice, hydrocarbons and silicates, along with other solid material. It comes from many places. Some is left over from the birth of stars and planets, and some consists of molecules that starlight has altered over millions of years.

NGC 3169 lies about 70 million light-years away in the constellation Sextans (The Sextant). It belongs to the Leo I Group of galaxies. Like the Local Group that contains our Milky Way, the Leo I Group is one part of a much larger gathering called the Virgo Supercluster.
explore: The picture was released as an ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week. It was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through two filters, one tuned to a wavelength of 658 nanometres and one to 814 nanometres in the near-infrared.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 3169 in visible red and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: One of the filters records near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and a galaxy this far away is far too faint for unaided eyes.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen at a sharp angle, its bright centre partly hidden behind thick dust in its spiral arms.

caption: Part of the Carina Nebula around the star WR 22, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This wide picture covers part of the Carina Nebula and is centred on WR 22, an unusual star that is hot, massive and young. A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space, and this one is so large that the frame shows only part of it.
WR 22 belongs to a rare group called Wolf–Rayet stars. Stars like this are massive and very hot, and they drive strong winds of gas away from their surfaces.

The Carina Nebula lies about 7500 light-years away. At that distance the patch of sky shown, 0.55 by 0.55 degrees, spans a region about 72 light-years on each side. The picture was assembled from exposures through red, green and blue filters taken with the Wide Field Imager, a camera on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.
explore: The object list for this picture also includes Eta Carinae, another massive star in the Carina Nebula, although ESO does not point it out in the frame or say where it sits relative to WR 22.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla recorded this scene in visible light through blue, green (V) and red filters, which ESO combined into a colour picture.
understand.eye: The camera builds up faint nebular light over long exposures, so the nebula appears far brighter and more detailed than it would to the eye.

alt: A wide view of part of the Carina Nebula centred on the hot, massive star WR 22.

caption: The central area of the giant elliptical galaxy NGC 1316, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: Dark clouds and lanes of dust cross the heart of NGC 1316. This giant elliptical galaxy belongs to the Fornax cluster of galaxies. Scattered around it are objects that look like stars, and some of them are in fact globular clusters, dense balls of stars that belong to the galaxy.

Elliptical galaxies are usually smooth, rounded collections of stars with little dust, so the many dust clouds in the centre of NGC 1316 make it stand out. The globular clusters around it are part of the galaxy's own family of stars.

Some features come from the camera, not the sky. Pyramid shapes above and below the bright centre, and straight vertical streaks through several of the brightest stars, appear because those parts of the detector were overexposed, an effect known as CCD bleeding. The picture uses exposures from the 8.2-m VLT ANTU telescope and its FORS-1 instrument, taken through B, V and I filters that are rendered in blue, green-yellow and red.
explore: The field measures 6.8 by 6.8 arcminutes, with 0.2 arcseconds per pixel, and the image quality of the composite is about 0.9 arcseconds. North is up and east is to the left. NGC 1316 lies about 60 million light-years away.

understand.summary: The FORS-1 instrument on the 8.2-m VLT ANTU telescope recorded NGC 1316 through B, V and I filters. B is shown as blue, V as green-yellow and the near-infrared I filter as red.
understand.eye: The I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the camera gathers far more light than the eye, so dust lanes and faint clusters stand out clearly.

alt: The bright centre of a giant elliptical galaxy crossed by dark dust lanes, with star-like globular clusters around it and pyramid-shaped overexposure artefacts above and below the centre.

caption: The galaxy cluster PLCKESZ G286.6-31.3 behind the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: A starry field fills this picture, and the galaxy cluster PLCKESZ G286.6-31.3 hides among the stars. It is hard to pick out at first but shows up as a faint grouping of yellowish galaxies close to the middle of the frame. At lower left sits IC 2140, a globular star cluster.
The cluster contains up to 1000 galaxies, along with large amounts of hot gas and dark matter. Altogether its mass comes to 530 trillion times that of the Sun.

From Earth we see the cluster through the outer edges of the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the Milky Way's satellite galaxies. That is why the field is so crowded. Most of the objects in the frame are stars and star clusters inside the Large Magellanic Cloud, home to over 700 star clusters as well as giant and supergiant stars numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
explore: The picture comes from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, which has worked at ESO's La Silla Observatory since 1984 and has been used in research into gamma-ray bursts. The 67-million-pixel camera has been photographing faint, distant objects since 1999. The data were chosen from the ESO archive for the Hidden Treasures competition.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope observed this field in visible and near-infrared light through V, R and I filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the cluster's galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

alt: A crowded star field with a faint group of yellowish galaxies near the centre and a globular star cluster at lower left.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4907, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: We see NGC 4907 face-on, its spiral arms wound loosely around a bright central bar of stars. Below the galaxy shines a single star, and several other galaxies appear around it. NGC 4907 is a barred spiral about 270 million light-years away, visible to observers in the northern hemisphere.

The bright star below the galaxy is not part of it. It lies within our own Milky Way, only 2500 light-years away and so 100 000 times closer than NGC 4907. Its nearness makes it look brighter than the many millions of stars in the galaxy behind it.

NGC 4907 belongs to the Coma Cluster, which holds over 1000 galaxies, and some of its neighbours share the frame. The cluster lies within the constellation Coma Berenices, whose name refers to the hair of Queen Berenice II of Egypt.
explore: Coma Berenices is the only constellation named after a historical person. The picture was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 through two long-pass filters, both of which record visible light.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 4907 through two long-pass filters in visible light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope, and Hubble's long exposures gather far more light than the eye can.

alt: A face-on barred spiral galaxy with loosely wound arms, a bright foreground star below it and other galaxies scattered around.

caption: Laser guide stars above the Residencia, Paranal Observatory
story: Orange laser beams rise from Cerro Paranal into the night sky in this photograph, taken from just outside the Residencia, ESO's hotel for staff at Paranal Observatory. In the distance stands the rough outline of the Very Large Telescope (VLT) on the mountaintop, where one of the Unit Telescopes is firing its 4 Laser Guide Star Facility.

Near the ends of the beams a bright orange dot sits slightly apart from them. It looks like one point but is really four artificial stars. Each laser excites sodium atoms 90 km above the ground and makes them glow. With these artificial stars the VLT can correct for the blurring caused by turbulence in the atmosphere, which lets it produce very sharp images.
The Residencia, built in 2002, gives astronomers, engineers and other staff a place to rest, sheltered from the harsh conditions of the Atacama Desert.
explore: The Residencia is well known beyond astronomy. The building appeared in the James Bond film Quantum of Solace. The photograph was published as an ESO Picture of the Week, taken by N. Schafer.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of Paranal Observatory at night, showing the laser beams of the VLT's 4 Laser Guide Star Facility. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the beams and the night sky may look brighter than they would to someone standing there.

alt: Orange laser beams rising from the Very Large Telescope on a distant mountaintop into the night sky, seen from outside the Residencia building.

caption: The interacting galaxy pair Zw I 136 and its neighbours, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Galaxies of many colours and shapes crowd this Hubble frame. Some are bright and nearby, some are fuzzy, and some are so far off that they show up only as small specks. The two on the left stand out. At the bottom is 2MASX J16133219+5103436, and above it is its blue-tinted companion SDSS J161330.18+510335.

Together the two form a pair called Zw I 136. The upper galaxy is slightly closer to us, but they are near enough to each other to interact. Both have disturbed shapes and extended soft halos, unlike the third bright object in the frame, a spiral seen edge-on toward the right.

Pairs like this help with a central question in the study of how galaxies change over time. Astronomers want to know how encounters between galaxies set off waves of star formation, and why that star formation then stops abruptly.
explore: Astronomers sort galaxies by their appearance and shape. The best-known scheme is the Hubble sequence, devised by Edwin Hubble. Judy Schmidt entered a version of this picture into the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this field in ultraviolet, blue and red light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet filter records light the eye cannot see, and these galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

alt: Many galaxies of different colours and shapes, with two disturbed galaxies on the left, the upper one blue-tinted, and an edge-on spiral on the right.

caption: The dwarf galaxy ESO 489-056, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: At the centre of this Hubble frame, two spiral galaxies seem to be crashing together while a crowd of stars scatters from the scene. The impression is a trick of perspective. Two spirals are indeed colliding, but they lie millions of light-years beyond the cloud of blue and red stars that seems to be fleeing them.
That scattering of stars is a separate, irregular dwarf galaxy called ESO 489-056. Many bright stars in the frame are much closer still, in the foreground within our own Milky Way.

ESO 489-056 lies 16 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Canis Major (The Greater Dog). It holds a few billion red and blue stars. That is a small number next to the Milky Way, which is estimated to hold around 200 to 400 billion stars. The Andromeda Galaxy contains one trillion.
explore: The picture was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through a visible red filter and a near-infrared filter. Luca Limatola entered a version of it into the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed this field in visible red and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the dwarf galaxy's stars are far too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A cloud of blue and red stars in front of two colliding spiral galaxies, with bright foreground stars around them.

caption: The dwarf galaxy Pisces B, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows the galaxy Pisces B. Below and to the left of centre sits a bright object with spikes of light radiating from it. That object is not part of Pisces B but a foreground star in our own Milky Way. Several distant galaxies also appear in the background.
Pisces B is a dwarf galaxy, a small galaxy with far fewer stars than a large spiral like the Milky Way. It lies about 30 million light-years away.

The spikes around the bright star are diffraction spikes. They are not real features of the star. They appear because of the way a telescope's structure bends incoming light, and they tend to show up around bright point sources such as nearby stars. The fainter background galaxies lie far beyond Pisces B.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took the picture through two filters, one in visible light and one in the near-infrared. The object list also names Pisces B by its catalogue designation, [SCB2015] GALFA-Dw2.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed Pisces B in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and a dwarf galaxy this distant is far too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A faint dwarf galaxy with a bright foreground star showing diffraction spikes below left of centre and small distant galaxies in the background.

caption: Orion above ALMA antennas, ALMA Operations Support Facility, Chile
story: Three dish antennas belonging to ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, stand under the Chilean night sky, with the constellation Orion, the Hunter, shining high above them. Its hourglass outline and the three bright stars of Orion's Belt make it easy to recognise. Because the photo was taken from the southern hemisphere, Orion's sword appears above the Belt.
The middle "star" of the sword is really the Orion Nebula, whose fuzzy glow can be seen without a telescope when conditions are good.

The three antennas are a small part of ALMA, which has 66 antennas in total. By combining signals from antennas spread up to 16 kilometres apart, a technique called interferometry, ALMA acts as a single giant telescope. When the photo was taken, the antennas were being tested at ALMA's Operations Support Facility, which sits lower, at 2900 metres. After testing and fitting out, the antennas were moved up to the Chajnantor plateau at 5000 metres, one of the driest places in the world.
explore: ALMA observes at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which water vapour and oxygen in Earth's atmosphere strongly absorb, so it needs a high, dry site. Early science observations began with part of the array late in 2011. Adrian Russell took the photo and shared it in the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group. ALMA is run jointly by Europe, North America and East Asia, working with the Republic of Chile.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of ALMA antennas at night with the constellation Orion overhead. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can gather more light than the eye, so the stars may look richer than they would to someone standing beside the antennas.

alt: Three large dish antennas under a starry night sky, with the constellation Orion high above them.

caption: The galaxy cluster RXC J0142.9+4438, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Galaxies fill this Hubble frame. Spiral arms turn in every colour and direction, and fuzzy elliptical galaxies appear as soft, glowing smudges. A few stars much closer to home shine brightly in the foreground. At the very centre sits a massive galaxy cluster, RXC J0142.9+4438, a gathering of perhaps thousands of galaxies held together by gravity.

Every speck of a galaxy contains countless stars. Clusters like this one mark the knots of the cosmic web, the large-scale structure that runs through the Universe, so studying them means studying how matter is organised on the largest scales.

Clusters are useful for work on dark matter and dark energy, and they help astronomers reach galaxies far beyond them. Their gravity is so strong that it bends the spacetime around them, making the cluster behave like an enormous zoom lens. Light from galaxies behind the cluster gets warped and magnified on its way to us, giving a view of the distant, and therefore early, Universe.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 took this picture for an observing programme called RELICS, the Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey. The survey covered 41 massive galaxy clusters, looking for the brightest distant galaxies for the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope to study.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed this cluster in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

alt: Many spiral and fuzzy elliptical galaxies of different colours scattered across a dark field, with a few bright foreground stars and a dense cluster of galaxies at the centre.

caption: The merged galaxy NGC 7727, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: The galaxy NGC 7727 has a wispy shape, the result of two galaxies merging. Their merger began around a billion years ago, and NGC 7727 is what the pair has become.

When galaxies merge, their gravity pulls stars and gas out of their original orbits, leaving loose, irregular structures like the wisps around this one. Each large galaxy is thought to hold a supermassive black hole at its centre, and a merger brings those black holes together too.

That is happening deep inside NGC 7727. Two supermassive black holes are spiralling toward each other in the galaxy's core. They are expected to merge within 250 million years. That sounds like a long wait, but on the timescales that galaxies live by, it is very short. The galaxy lies about 90 million light-years away, and this picture comes from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT).
explore: FORS2 stands for FOcal Reducer and low dispersion Spectrograph 2. For this picture it recorded the galaxy through three visible-light filters, centred on blue, green and red wavelengths of 440, 557 and 655 nanometres.

understand.summary: The FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope recorded NGC 7727 in visible light through blue, green and red filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The VLT's large mirror and long exposures gather far more light than the eye, which is why faint wisps around the galaxy show up.

alt: A galaxy with a wispy, irregular shape formed by the merger of two galaxies.

caption: The galaxy NGC 2442, host of supernova SN2015F, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows NGC 2442, a galaxy nicknamed the Meathook Galaxy because its shape is so lopsided and irregular. In March 2015 it hosted a supernova, a star explosion called SN2015F.

The explosion began with a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a star, in a binary star system. The white dwarf drew mass away from its companion star and kept doing so until it had taken on more than it could hold. That knocked the star off balance and set off runaway nuclear fusion, which led to a violent supernova.

SN2015F stayed bright for a long time. Through even a small telescope it was easy to see from Earth until later that summer. NGC 2442 itself lies about 55 million light-years away, and its distorted outline is what earned it the nickname.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 made this picture through four filters that span blue, green, red and near-infrared light. The observations are credited to S. Smartt and colleagues, and the image was released as an ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 2442 in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: One filter records near-infrared light that the eye cannot see, and the galaxy's faint structure needs Hubble's light-gathering power to show up.

alt: The irregular, lopsided galaxy NGC 2442, which hosted the supernova SN2015F.

caption: The star cluster RCW 38, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This picture shows RCW 38, a dense cluster of stars about 5,500 light-years away, seen toward the constellation Vela (the Sails).

Astronomers call RCW 38 an "embedded" cluster. Its stars are still wrapped in the cloud of dust and gas they formed from. A cluster like this is young, because over time stars clear away the cloud that gave birth to them. Inside it, young and very powerful stars blast newborn suns and planets with strong winds and intense light. Massive, short-lived stars add to the assault when they explode as supernovae. Sometimes this barrage boils away material that might one day have formed new planetary systems.
Scientists think our own Solar System may have come out of a similarly harsh place. Clusters like RCW 38 help show what that early setting could have been like.
explore: ESO built the picture from Wide Field Imager data recorded through four filters, B, V, R and H-alpha. That camera belongs to the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, which stands at La Silla, and the frame spans roughly 10 arcminutes.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla recorded RCW 38 in visible light through B, V, R and H-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera builds up light over long exposures, so the cluster and its surrounding cloud look far brighter and more detailed than they would to the eye.

alt: The dense star cluster RCW 38, still embedded in its cloud of dust and gas.

caption: Part of the Serpens Nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope with HAWK-I
story: Young red stars, reflection nebulae and dark clouds of dust and gas all stand out clearly in this infrared close-up of a young star-forming region in Serpens. The region is thought to be only about a million years old.

The picture comes from detector 1 of HAWK-I, an infrared camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The exposures were short, just 1 minute per filter through three infrared filters, and still the image records a great deal of detail.

Reflection nebulae are clouds of dust that shine by scattering the light of nearby stars. Dark clouds are dense enough to block the light of whatever lies behind them. Infrared light passes through dust more easily than visible light does, which helps a camera like HAWK-I pick out young stars that are still surrounded by the material they formed from. The Serpens Nebula lies about 1000 light-years away.
explore: HAWK-I observed through the J, H and K infrared filters. This frame is a close-up from detector 1, just one of the camera's detectors, which is why it shows only part of the region.

understand.summary: HAWK-I on ESO's Very Large Telescope recorded this region in near-infrared light through J, H and K filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so this view shows young stars and dust structures that could not be seen directly.

alt: Red young stars, reflection nebulae and dark clouds of gas and dust in a star-forming region in Serpens.

caption: A meteor above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal
story: A meteoroid flares across the night sky above Paranal in the Chilean desert, ending its journey through the Solar System in a burst of light. Three Unit Telescopes and one Auxiliary Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) stand below it. A diffuse red glow spreads across the sky, light given off by oxygen and nitrogen in Earth's atmosphere.

Meteoroids are rocky objects smaller than asteroids that drift through space. When one enters Earth's atmosphere, friction with the air heats it until it vaporises, leaving a glowing streak called a meteor, or shooting star. Any part that survives and reaches the ground is called a meteorite.
The colour of a meteor's trail shows what the meteoroid was made of. Green light points to magnesium, and yellow light points to iron.
explore: The VLT is made up of four Unit Telescopes plus four Auxiliary Telescopes that can be moved. These movable ones work together as the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, which combines their light for much finer detail, and the Unit Telescopes can join in. The VLT produced the first image of a planet outside the Solar System and has tracked stars orbiting the supermassive black hole at the centre of our galaxy.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of the VLT at Paranal at night, showing a meteor and airglow. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: The camera catches colours and faint airglow that a watcher on the ground might barely notice, since the eye sees little colour in dim light.

alt: A bright meteor streaking across the night sky above three large telescope domes and a smaller one, with a diffuse red glow across the sky.

caption: The interacting galaxy Markarian 231, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright, star-like glow shines at the centre of Markarian 231 in this Hubble picture. Markarian 231 is an interacting galaxy and the nearest quasar to Earth, 600 million light-years away. Its light set out so long ago that it shows the galaxy as it was before multicelled life arose on Earth.

A quasar is powered by a black hole at a galaxy's centre, which heats the surrounding gas until it releases enormous amounts of energy. Spectroscopic observations with Hubble suggest that Markarian 231 holds not one but two supermassive black holes, circling each other.

If the closest quasar has such a pair, that would imply many quasars host binary black holes. Such a pair would be a natural outcome of two galaxies merging, each bringing its own central black hole. That idea rests on this one example, so it remains an inference rather than a settled fact.
explore: The picture was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. It is credited to the Hubble Heritage Team and A. Evans of the University of Virginia, NRAO and Stony Brook University.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed Markarian 231 in blue visible light and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and a galaxy this far away is far too faint for the unaided eye.

caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 271, imaged by the New Technology Telescope
story: Two spiral galaxies of similar size, NGC 5426 and NGC 5427, are caught in a slow gravitational encounter, linked by a bridge of stars that already joins them. Together they are known as Arp 271.

The two galaxies have already been changed by their meeting, although it is not certain that they will go on to collide and merge. The encounter will last for tens of millions of years, and their mutual pull will trigger the birth of new stars along the way. The bridge of stars between them is a visible sign of that pull.

Arp 271 lies 90 million light-years away toward the constellation Virgo (the Virgin) and spans about 130 000 light-years. William Herschel first discovered it in 1785. Our own Milky Way may go through a similar collision with the neighbouring Andromeda galaxy in about five billion years. Andromeda is now about 2.6 million light-years away.
explore: ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile is home to the 3.58-metre New Technology Telescope, and its EFOSC instrument took the picture. Data were collected through B, V and R filters for a total exposure time of 4440 seconds, and the field of view is about 4 arcminutes.

understand.summary: The EFOSC instrument on ESO's 3.58-metre New Technology Telescope recorded Arp 271 in visible light through B, V and R filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: A total exposure time of 4440 seconds gathers far more light than the eye can, so the faint bridge of stars shows up.

caption: The zodiacal light above the Very Large Telescope's laser guide stars, Paranal
story: The lasers of the 4 Laser Guide Star Facility on ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) appear to point toward a soft bluish band in the sky. That band is the zodiacal light, sunlight scattered by dust grains left over from collisions between asteroids and from the tails of comets.

Blue light scatters more easily than red light, the same reason the daytime sky is blue, so the zodiacal light looks bluish. It follows the line of the zodiac constellations, which runs along the ecliptic, the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun, and that is where its name comes from.

People call it a false dawn or false dusk. It does not come from our atmosphere, and it appears just before sunrise and just after sunset. Light pollution has made it hard to see in many places, but Chile's Atacama Desert still has some of the darkest skies in the world.
explore: The zodiacal light is easiest to see where the ecliptic rides high in the sky. In the Southern Hemisphere that means late evenings from January to April and early mornings from September to November, with the pattern reversed in the Northern Hemisphere.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of the VLT's laser guide stars and the zodiacal light at Paranal. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: The zodiacal light is faint, and a long camera exposure can make it look brighter and bluer than it appears to the eye.

alt: Laser beams from a telescope on a mountaintop pointing toward a diffuse bluish band of light in the night sky.

caption: The spiral galaxy PGC 54493, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows PGC 54493, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Serpens (The Serpent). It belongs to a cluster of galaxies that astronomers have studied for a subtle effect called weak gravitational lensing.

Weak lensing happens because matter, dark matter included, is spread unevenly through the Universe. Its gravity slightly bends light from distant galaxies, adding tiny distortions to their images. That particular distortion is called cosmic shear, and PGC 54493 has been studied in connection with it. Surveys such as the Hubble Medium Deep Survey have looked for this effect.

Dark matter is one of cosmology's great puzzles. It neither gives off nor absorbs light or any other electromagnetic energy, which is why it is called dark. Astronomers still know it is there. Galaxies spin so fast, and in such a way, that the ordinary matter we can see could not hold them together. The missing mass is dark matter, thought to make up some 27% of everything in the Universe.
explore: Dark energy and normal matter make up the rest of the Universe's contents. The mismatch between how galaxies rotate and how much visible matter they contain is known as the galaxy rotation problem. Judy Schmidt entered a version of this picture into the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed PGC 54493 through three filters in blue-green visible light and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Two of the filters record near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to see without a large telescope.

caption: The globular star cluster Messier 4, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This picture from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory shows Messier 4, a globular star cluster. It is one of the closest clusters of its kind to Earth, lying about 7000 light-years away.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical ball of very old stars, held together by their shared gravity. Messier 4 is a great ball of ancient stars of this kind. Clusters like it orbit in the outer halos of galaxies such as our own, and because their stars formed long ago, astronomers use them to study a galaxy's early history.
On the sky, Messier 4 appears in the constellation Scorpius (The Scorpion), near Antares, a bright red star. The data for this picture come from the ESO Imaging Survey.
explore: Messier 4 is also catalogued as M 4 and NGC 6121. The Wide Field Imager recorded it through three filters, two in visible light and one in the near-infrared, at wavelengths of 456, 540 and 784 nanometres.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope observed Messier 4 through blue, green and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the camera gathers far more light than the eye, so many more faint stars appear.

alt: The globular star cluster Messier 4, a dense ball of old stars.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: At the heart of this Webb mosaic, massive young stars glitter pale blue in the Tarantula Nebula's most active region. Scattered among them are red stars still buried in the dusty cocoon of the nebula. Farther from the core, cooler gas takes on a rust colour. The mosaic, from Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), reveals tens of thousands of young stars that dust had hidden until now.

NIRCam can pick out these dust-shrouded stars because of its very sharp resolution in near-infrared light. Above and to the left of the young cluster, an older star shows the eight diffraction spikes typical of NIRCam, an effect of the telescope's structure. Its upper central spike almost points to a bubble in the cloud, blown by young stars that are still wrapped in dust and have begun carving out a cavity of their own.
The rust colour tells astronomers the nebula is rich in complex hydrocarbons. That dense gas is the raw material for future stars.
explore: Astronomers turned two of Webb's spectrographs on the region to work out what the star and the gas around it are made of. Those spectra should tell astronomers how old the nebula is and how many rounds of star formation it has been through. As winds from massive stars sweep gas and dust aside, some of it will pile up and, with help from gravity, form new stars.

understand.summary: Webb's Near-Infrared Camera recorded the Tarantula Nebula in near-infrared light. The release explains what the pale blue, red and rust colours show, but the filter-to-colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes through dust that hides many of these young stars in visible light.

scaleExtra: The mosaic stretches 340 light-years across, according to ESA/Webb.
alt: A glowing cavity of gas with pale blue young stars at its centre, red dust-embedded stars among them, a star with eight diffraction spikes at upper left, and rust-coloured gas farther out.

caption: The jellyfish galaxy NGC 3312 in the Hydra I cluster, imaged by ESO
story: Right at the centre of this frame, the spiral galaxy NGC 3312 looks almost smeared across the view, as if spilling its contents into the space around it. The frame shows a small part of the Hydra I cluster, which holds hundreds of galaxies, and NGC 3312 is the largest spiral galaxy known in that cluster.

The smudged look comes from a process called ram pressure stripping. A galaxy moving through a dense fluid, such as the hot gas that fills the space between galaxies in a cluster, feels that gas dragging on the colder gas in its outer layers. The drag pulls the cold gas away and lets it leak out.

Cold gas is what stars form from, so a galaxy that loses it this way risks a shrinking population of stars. Affected galaxies, usually ones falling toward the centre of a cluster, tend to end up with long tendrils of gas trailing behind them. That appearance gives them the nickname jellyfish galaxies.
explore: The picture was released as an ESO Picture of the Week and is credited to ESO, INAF, M. Spavone and E. Iodice. Besides NGC 3312, the frame holds hundreds of other small blips, and each galaxy in the cluster has its own history.

understand.summary: ESO does not name the telescope, instrument or filters used for this picture, and the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxy and its stripped gas are far too faint to see with the eye, and a telescope exposure gathers much more light.

alt: A spiral galaxy at the centre of the frame that looks smeared out, surrounded by many small points of light from other galaxies.

caption: Stephan's Quintet, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars of a wide range of colours, from young blue stars to ageing red ones, fill this Hubble portrait of Stephan's Quintet, also called Hickson Compact Group 92. Three of the galaxies have distorted shapes, stretched spiral arms and long tidal tails of gas full of star clusters, signs of close encounters.

The name is slightly misleading. NGC 7320, at upper left, is a foreground galaxy about seven times closer than the rest. It lies 40 million light-years away, while the other members, in the constellation Pegasus, are about 300 million light-years distant. Hubble can pick out single stars in NGC 7320 but not in most of the Quintet.

The collisions have set off a burst of star birth in the two central galaxies. Circling them are bright young blue star clusters and pink clouds of hydrogen gas that glow where stars less than 10 million years old are forming. The colours trace stars of different ages, showing that star birth happened at different times over hundreds of millions of years.
explore: The barred spiral NGC 7319, at top right, has arms that reach nearly 180 degrees back to the bar. What looks like one galaxy with two cores is really NGC 7318A and NGC 7318B. NGC 7317, at bottom left, is an elliptical less touched by the encounters. Edouard M. Stephan spotted the group in 1877, the first compact group ever found.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the Quintet in visible and near-infrared light, using filters for blue, green and infrared light and for glowing ionised hydrogen. Which colour each filter was assigned isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera's infrared view looks through dust to show star groups that cannot be seen in visible light, and the eye cannot see infrared at all.

alt: A group of galaxies with distorted shapes and long tails, dotted with blue star clusters and pink glowing clouds, and a closer galaxy at upper left.

caption: Alpha Centauri and Beta Centauri in the constellation Centaurus, La Silla Observatory
story: Alpha Centauri and Beta Centauri sit at the centre of this photograph of the constellation Centaurus, taken at ESO's La Silla Observatory. Each of the two is a triple star system.

A triple system is a group of three stars bound together by gravity, and systems with more than one star are common in our galaxy. In each of these two, the brightest stars orbit close to one another. Seen from Earth, those companions are too close together to separate by eye, so each system looks like a single point of light.

Apart from the Sun, Alpha Centauri is the nearest "star" to Earth. The word is in quotation marks because the point we see is more than one star. A constellation is a pattern of stars as seen from Earth, and its stars usually lie at very different distances from us. The photographer is Zdeněk Bardon, and ESO published the picture.

understand.summary: This is a wide-field photograph of the constellation Centaurus taken at La Silla Observatory. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so many more faint stars may show than a watcher would see.

alt: A starry sky in the constellation Centaurus with Alpha Centauri and Beta Centauri at the centre.

caption: A spiral arm of the Milky Way around the Eta Carinae Nebula, photographed by Zdeněk Bardon for ESO
story: Stars and glowing gas and dust from one of the Milky Way's spiral arms fill this photograph. At its centre lies the Eta Carinae nebula, in the southern constellation Carina (the Keel).

The Milky Way, our own galaxy, is a spiral galaxy. Its stars, gas and dust are gathered into a flat disc with arms that wind outward from the centre. Because we live inside that disc, we never see the spiral shape from above. From inside, we see the stars, gas and dust of the arms spread across our sky.

A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space, and some nebulae shine because nearby stars light them up. The Eta Carinae nebula is an emission nebula, a cloud of hydrogen gas that glows because hot stars nearby energise it. The photograph was taken by Zdeněk Bardon and published by ESO.

understand.summary: This is a wide-field photograph of part of the Milky Way in Carina. No camera settings or site are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the glowing gas and faint stars look much brighter than they would to a watcher.

alt: Stars and glowing gas and dust from one of the Milky Way's spiral arms, with the Eta Carinae nebula at the centre.

caption: The Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: This picture from ESO's VISTA telescope shows the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the galaxies closest to our own.

VISTA has been surveying the Large Magellanic Cloud, its sibling the Small Magellanic Cloud and the region around both in great detail. A nearby galaxy seen whole is a useful laboratory. Its stars are all at roughly the same distance from us, which makes them easier to compare than stars scattered through our own Milky Way.

Because the survey captures a huge number of stars, it opens up new ways to study how stars change over their lives, how galaxies move and hold together, and variable stars, whose brightness changes over time. VISTA observes in infrared light, which helps it see through dust that would hide stars at visible wavelengths.
explore: The picture comes from the VMC survey and was made with VISTA's VIRCAM camera through three near-infrared filters, called Y, J and Ks, at wavelengths of 1.02, 1.25 and 2.15 micrometres.

understand.summary: VISTA's VIRCAM camera observed the Large Magellanic Cloud in near-infrared light through Y, J and Ks filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so this view is not what anyone would see looking at the Large Magellanic Cloud in the night sky.

alt: The Large Magellanic Cloud seen in infrared light by the VISTA telescope.

caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 6872 and IC 4970, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 6872 has an unusual shape, and the cause sits just above it in this Hubble picture, a smaller galaxy called IC 4970. NGC 6872's upper left spiral arm is clearly bent out of shape and dotted with star-forming regions that appear blue. The pair lies in the constellation Pavo (The Peacock), roughly 300 million light-years from Earth.

The distortion may have come from IC 4970 passing through that arm about 130 million years ago, which counts as recent for galaxies. NGC 6872 seems to hold relatively little free hydrogen, the raw material for new stars. Without its encounter with IC 4970, it might have been unable to start fresh bursts of star formation.
NGC 6872 is enormous. From tip to tip it measures over 500 000 light-years, making it the second largest spiral galaxy found so far. Only NGC 262, at 1.3 million light-years, is bigger.
explore: Our own Milky Way spans between 100 000 and 120 000 light-years, so NGC 6872 is about five times its size. Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 took the picture, and Judy Schmidt entered a version of it in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 observed NGC 6872 in visible and near-infrared light. Star-forming regions appear blue, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and galaxies this distant are far too faint for the unaided eye.

alt: A large spiral galaxy with a distorted upper left arm dotted with blue star-forming regions, and a smaller galaxy just above it.

caption: Dust pillars in the Carina Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Tall pillars of cold hydrogen and dust rise in the Carina Nebula in this Hubble picture, each one about a light-year high. Like ice cream melting out of shape on a hot summer day, they are being worn away, in this case by radiation from massive stars.

Fierce stellar winds and strong radiation from those stars are carving away at cold molecular clouds, sculpting the surrounding nebula into strange, fantasy-like forms. Inside these dense structures, new stars may form.

The Carina Nebula lies in the southern constellation Carina, an estimated 7,500 light-years away. Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys built this composite from two sets of observations. The 2005 data record hydrogen light, given off by hydrogen atoms, and the 2010 data record oxygen light, given off by oxygen atoms.
explore: The two filters used pick out narrow wavelengths, one at 502 nanometres for glowing oxygen and one at 658 nanometres for hydrogen and nitrogen. The picture is credited to the Hubble Heritage Project, with thanks to M. Livio and N. Smith.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the pillars through narrow filters that isolate light from glowing hydrogen and oxygen. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate light from single chemical elements, and the nebula is far too faint for the eye to see in this detail.

alt: Tall pillars of cold hydrogen gas and dust in the Carina Nebula.

caption: The galaxies NGC 4858 and NGC 4860 in the Coma Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two galaxies dominate this Hubble frame. The brighter one, at the centre, is NGC 4860, an elliptical galaxy. To its left is NGC 4858, a spiral with a tangled, fiery look. Both belong to the Coma Cluster in the northern constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair), where more than a thousand galaxies are held together by gravity.

Many of the cluster's members are ellipticals, but its outer parts also hold younger spirals. NGC 4858 is an unusual case. Astronomers call it a galaxy aggregate, a central galaxy ringed by a few bright knots of material that seem to grow out of it, stretching and breaking away and reshaping it as they go.

It is also forming stars at a very high rate, possibly set off by an earlier encounter with another galaxy. At this pace it will run out of gas long before the end of its life. Its knots glow bright red, the colour of hydrogen gas energised by the many hot young stars inside them.
explore: The picture comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, an instrument designed to study how stars and galaxies developed in the early Universe. The two galaxies lie about 300 million light-years away.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded this pair through very broad filters in visible light. The red knots are glowing hydrogen, but the filter-to-colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope, and Hubble's exposures gather much more light than the eye.

alt: A bright elliptical galaxy at the centre with a smaller, tangled spiral galaxy to its left dotted with bright red knots.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4634, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble sees the spiral galaxy NGC 4634 exactly edge-on. Clear dust lanes and bright pink nebulae cross its disc, which is slightly warped. The nebulae run along the whole length of the galaxy and appear in parts of its halo, while dark threads of cold dust block some of the starlight.

The warp comes from an ongoing encounter with a nearby galaxy, NGC 4633, which lies just beyond the upper right corner of the frame. As galaxies approach each other, gravity pulls their tidy spiral shapes out of line and disturbs their gas clouds, which sets off bursts of star formation.

From this side-on angle the spiral pattern cannot be seen, but the signs of star birth are plain. The pink nebulae are gas clouds slowly gathering into stars, much like the Orion Nebula in our own galaxy. Radiation from the new stars makes the gas glow like a fluorescent sign. So many star-forming regions point to a gravitational interaction.
explore: NGC 4634 lies around 70 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. The picture combines visible-light exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and its Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 recorded NGC 4634 in visible light, including a filter for glowing hydrogen. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope, and Hubble's sharp exposures show dust lanes and nebulae the eye could not pick out.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a slightly warped disc, crossed by dark dust lanes and dotted with bright pink nebulae.

caption: The night sky above Paranal Observatory, seen from VISTA
story: The plane of the Milky Way shines brightly over Paranal Observatory in this night photograph. The orange speck of Mars sits at left, the magenta patch of the Carina Nebula glows at upper middle, and the starry constellations Scorpius and Orion are also in view. A row of lamps runs through the centre of the frame, lighting the path between the Very Large Telescope and VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, where the photo was taken.
ESO's sites in Chile at Paranal, La Silla and Chajnantor have very little light pollution. Still, the sky over them is rarely pitch-black.

The very sensitive camera also picked up airglow, the faint light given off by Earth's atmosphere, which colours the sky here with deep red and green tones. Airglow means that no observatory on Earth can ever be completely dark, although ESO's sites come close.
explore: Astronomer and photographer Yuri Beletsky took the picture as part of the 2016 ESO Fulldome Expedition team. The team travelled to Chile to collect images for the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Centre.

understand.summary: This is a night-sky photograph taken at Paranal Observatory with a highly sensitive camera. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: The sensitive camera records the colours of airglow and faint nebulae that the eye sees only dimly, if at all, at night.

alt: The Milky Way shining over Paranal Observatory at night, with an orange dot of Mars at left, a magenta nebula at upper middle, a line of small lamps in the centre and a sky tinted red and green by airglow.

caption: The New Technology Telescope at sunset, La Silla Observatory
story: The Sun has just dipped below the horizon at the left of this photograph, soaking the clouds in rich orange light, while the Moon already shines high overhead. The building is ESO's New Technology Telescope (NTT) at La Silla Observatory, in the Norte Chico region on the edge of the Chilean Atacama Desert. The last warm rays catch the reflective walls of its enclosure.

That shiny metal dome has a job. It keeps the enclosure from heating up during the day. Warm air rising around a telescope causes turbulence that blurs images and worsens what astronomers call seeing, the steadiness of the view through the atmosphere.
The dome is only one part of the effort to stay cool. The concrete platforms and parking areas around the site are painted white so that they reflect more sunlight and soak up less heat.
explore: The photograph was taken by B. Tafreshi and published by ESO. La Silla lies in the Norte Chico, on the outskirts of the Atacama Desert, where the dome's heat-reducing design matters during long sunny days.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of the New Technology Telescope taken just after sunset. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera can record colours and brightness differently from the eye, so the sunset glow may not look exactly as it would to someone standing there.

alt: A telescope building with reflective metal walls catching orange sunset light, orange clouds at left and a bright Moon overhead.

caption: The Hubble Ultra Deep Field, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Nearly 10,000 galaxies fill the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, and they come in many ages, sizes, shapes and colours. The larger, brighter and clearly defined spirals and ellipticals are the nearest ones. The smallest and reddest, about 100 of them, may be among the most distant galaxies known.

Looking far across space also means looking back in time, because light takes time to reach us. Those faint red galaxies may date from a time when the Universe was only 800 million years old. The nearest galaxies in the field flourished about 1 billion years ago, at a time when the cosmos had reached an age of 13 billion years.

Such a deep view took patience. Hubble made 800 exposures over 400 orbits around Earth, adding up to 11.3 days of total exposure time. Staring at one small patch of sky for so long lets a telescope gather light from galaxies far too faint to show up in a short exposure.
explore: The observations were made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The picture is credited to S. Beckwith and the HUDF Team. The field lies in the constellation Fornax.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the Ultra Deep Field through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The total exposure of 11.3 days gathers vastly more light than the eye ever could, and the near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see.

alt: A dark field crowded with thousands of galaxies of many shapes, sizes and colours, from large spirals and ellipticals to tiny red specks.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 22 in infrared, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: This infrared view from ESO's VISTA telescope shows Messier 22, a globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius. A globular cluster is a tightly packed group of very old stars, and Messier 22 lies about 10 000 light-years from us.

The picture was taken with VIRCAM, the infrared camera on VISTA (short for Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy). The image is one small piece of a much bigger project. It belongs to a record-breaking infrared map of our galaxy holding more than 1.5 billion objects.

Two surveys supplied the data, VVV (short for VISTA Variables in the Vía Láctea) and its follow-up, the VVV eXtended survey (VVVX). Mapping our galaxy in infrared light helps because infrared passes through dust that dims and hides stars at visible wavelengths.

understand.summary: VISTA's infrared camera VIRCAM recorded Messier 22 in infrared light for the VVV and VVVX surveys. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so this is not how Messier 22 would look through an ordinary telescope.

scaleExtra: Messier 22 lies about 10 000 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: An infrared view of the globular cluster Messier 22, a dense group of old stars.

caption: Gravitational arcs around the galaxy LRG-4-606, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Left of centre in this Hubble picture, distant blue galaxies have been pulled out into narrow, pale blue arcs. The arcs curve around a galaxy cluster centred on an object called LRG-4-606, and together they form a half-circle.

LRG stands for Luminous Red Galaxy, a label for a large set of bright red galaxies picked out by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Most are massive elliptical galaxies made of huge numbers of old stars. This frame must contain hundreds of billions of stars.

The arcs come from gravitational lensing. The cluster's gravity is strong enough to bend space itself and magnify light from galaxies much farther away. Lensing usually produces stretched-out arcs. The unusual part is that the galaxies here happen to be lined up so that the separate arcs join into a half-circle.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 supplied the exposures, taken in visible and near-infrared light, and the frame covers a patch of sky about 3 by 3 arcminutes. The picture is credited to ESA/Hubble and NASA.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this cluster in visible and near-infrared light. The lensed background galaxies appear blue, but the filter-to-colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and these faint arcs would be invisible without Hubble's long exposures.

alt: A galaxy cluster with narrow pale blue arcs left of centre that join into a half-circle.

caption: APEX and the Purico Complex at twilight, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Low twilight sunlight lights up the clouds over the Atacama landscape in deep red. The volcanic mountains of the Purico Complex fill much of the frame, with a highest peak reaching 5703 metres. On the remote road below, a single vehicle trails a plume of dust. Toward the left stands a cluster of buildings and a single antenna, the ESO-operated Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX).

APEX is one of the highest telescopes in the world, at 5100 metres on the Chajnantor plateau. It works at submillimetre wavelengths, which fall between infrared light and radio waves and help reveal some of the coldest and dustiest objects known, as well as some of the most distant.

Water vapour in Earth's atmosphere absorbs much of this radiation, so it is best observed from high, dry places, and the Atacama Desert is one of the driest on Earth. Over the years APEX has studied the early lives of massive galaxies and mapped the plane of the Milky Way.
explore: APEX has also studied matter torn apart by a supermassive black hole. The plateau is home to ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. Its 66 antennas are out of sight, spread across the plateau behind the photographer.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken at twilight on the Chajnantor plateau, showing APEX and the Purico Complex. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera can render colour and brightness differently from the eye, so the red twilight glow may not look exactly as it would to someone standing there.

alt: Volcanic mountains under red-lit twilight clouds, with a single vehicle raising dust on a road and a small group of buildings with one antenna at left.

caption: The spiral galaxy IC 5332, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy IC 5332 winds outward in fine detail in this Hubble picture. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 is sharp enough to separate the spiral arms from the dark patches of dust between them.

That dust blocks the ultraviolet and visible light that Hubble is sensitive to, so the patches show up as dark gaps. The stars, by contrast, stand out clearly, and their colours help astronomers tell younger stars from older ones and see how each group is spread across the galaxy.

This Hubble view is one half of a comparison. Webb's MIRI instrument gives a very different picture of the same galaxy, one that traces the patterns of gas spread across it. Hubble's ultraviolet and visible light picks out the stars, while Webb's mid-infrared view brings out the gas. Seeing a galaxy in more than one kind of light lets astronomers follow different parts of it.
explore: The picture is credited to ESA/Webb, NASA and CSA, J. Lee and the PHANGS-JWST and PHANGS-HST teams. The dust patches between the arms show up dark because they block the ultraviolet and visible light Hubble records.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded IC 5332 in ultraviolet and visible light. Purple shows 275 nm ultraviolet, blue shows 336 nm, cyan 438 nm, yellow 555 nm and red 814 nm light.
understand.eye: Part of this light is ultraviolet, which the eye cannot see, and the colours are assigned to separate filters rather than showing the galaxy's natural hue.

alt: A spiral galaxy with winding arms separated by dark patches of dust.
flags: caption also describes a Webb MIRI view not in this image

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1350, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1350 looks like a gigantic eye in this colour picture from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. Delicate structures show clearly within it, and many more distant galaxies appear in the background.

The picture comes from just 16 minutes of observations in total, combined into one colour composite. Colour composites like this are made by combining separate exposures taken through different filters, each one assigned its own colour.

A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust in which bright arms curl out from the centre. NGC 1350 is about 65 million light-years away. The faint background galaxies scattered around it lie far beyond it and appear small because of their great distance.
explore: FORS2 observed the galaxy through four filters, three in visible light (B, V and R) and one in the near-infrared (I). The picture is credited to ESO. The galaxy lies in the constellation Fornax.

understand.summary: The FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope recorded NGC 1350 through B, V, R and I filters, in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint for the unaided eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy shaped like a giant eye, with many small background galaxies around it.

caption: The jellyfish galaxy ESO 137-001, imaged by ALMA, the Very Large Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Knotty streams of gas pour out of the spiral galaxy ESO 137-001, giving it the look of a jellyfish. The tails, which trace hydrogen, glow bright purple, while orange-red flares mark hotspots of carbon oxide emission inside the system. Three observatories contributed. Hubble imaged the galaxy and its surroundings, the MUSE instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) recorded the tails, and ALMA spotted the hotspots.

The tails come from ram-pressure stripping. Inside a cluster, the space between galaxies is filled with material that behaves like a thick fluid, and as a galaxy ploughs through it, gas is torn out to form a trailing wake. ESO 137-001 sits in the Norma galaxy cluster, and the direction of its tail shows how it is moving. Galaxies usually fall toward a cluster's centre.

This is the first high-resolution map of cold molecular gas inside a galaxy undergoing this kind of stripping. It matters because the tails hold bursts of star formation called fireballs, and how stars form in such tails is still poorly understood.
explore: Among jellyfish galaxies, ESO 137-001 is one of the closest to Earth. ALMA, which made the cold-gas map, has 66 antennas and stands at 5000 metres on the Chajnantor plateau in Chile's Atacama Desert. The research is credited to P. Jachym of the Czech Academy of Sciences and colleagues.

understand.summary: This composite combines Hubble visible-light images of the galaxy, VLT MUSE observations of hydrogen shown in purple, and ALMA millimetre-wave observations of carbon oxide emission shown in orange-red.
understand.eye: ALMA's millimetre-wave light is invisible to the eye, and the purple and orange-red tones are colours assigned to show different gases.

alt: A spiral galaxy trailing long, knotty streams of bright purple gas, with orange-red flares scattered through the system.

caption: The rippled edge of the Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A thin sheet of gas at the edge of the Orion Nebula ripples like a window curtain in this early Hubble picture. The sheet glows in the light of sulfur atoms, shown in red, while light from oxygen and hydrogen, shown in blue and green, spreads more smoothly through the nebula's interior.

The sheet marks the boundary between the nebula's hot, thin interior and a neighbouring dense, cool cloud. Sulfur shines most strongly where conditions fall between those two extremes. Its glow breaks up into threads and clumps as small as the telescope can show.

The Orion Nebula, an estimated 1500 light-years away, is a stellar nursery. Intense ultraviolet light from a cluster of very hot, luminous stars powers its glow. The sulfur light comes from where that starlight is boiling material off the face of the dense cloud, the same cloud the hot stars formed from, where more stars are still forming.
explore: The picture was made with Hubble's Wide Field/Planetary Camera, built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Astronomers described it as a good example of how, despite the spherical aberration that hampered many of the telescope's planned programmes, Hubble could still return data far clearer than was usually possible from the ground.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field/Planetary Camera recorded light from glowing sulfur, oxygen and hydrogen. Sulfur is shown in red, oxygen in blue and hydrogen in green.
understand.eye: Each colour isolates light from one kind of atom, so this is a map of chemistry rather than the nebula's natural appearance to the eye.

alt: A rippled, curtain-like sheet of red-glowing gas along the edge of a smoother blue and green nebula.

caption: The Dumbbell Nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: In the constellation Vulpecula (The Fox) lies the Dumbbell Nebula, also catalogued as Messier 27 and NGC 6853, a typical example of a planetary nebula. Its hot central star is easy to see in this photo. Its distance is not well known, though it is believed to be around 1,200 light-years.

Despite the name, planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets. The Dumbbell is made of very thin gas thrown off by the central star, which is now in one of its last stages of life. Strong ultraviolet radiation from the star excites the gas atoms, and they shine brightly at particular wavelengths.

The picture came about as a by-product of a technical test of narrow-band filters for the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. Such filters let through only a narrow slice of wavelengths, isolating light from particular atoms and ions. Combining them with a broad blue filter gave the nebula's structure in approximately true colours.
explore: Charles Messier, a French astronomer and comet hunter, found the nebula in 1764 and listed it as number 27 in his catalogue. The exposures were taken during mediocre seeing of 0.8 arcseconds, with 5 minutes each through the oxygen and hydrogen filters and 30 seconds through the blue filter.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope recorded the nebula through a broad blue filter and narrow filters for doubly ionised oxygen and hydrogen. These were shown as blue, green and red to give approximately true colours.
understand.eye: The camera gathers far more light than the eye, so the nebula's faint structure appears much brighter than it would through an eyepiece.

alt: A glowing planetary nebula with a visible hot star at its centre.

caption: Star trails over the Paranal Residencia, Cerro Paranal
story: Star trails streak across a dark Chilean sky in this long-exposure photograph. As Earth turned during the exposure, each star traced a streak. Beneath them lies the Paranal Residencia, a refuge for staff and visitors at ESO's Very Large Telescope, high on Cerro Paranal in the Chilean desert.

Work on the Residencia began in 1998 and was finished by 2002. Since then it has given the scientists and engineers of Paranal Observatory a break from the harsh, dry desert climate. Most of the four-storey building lies underground.

German architects Auer+Weber designed it to blend with its surroundings. From some angles, the mix of high-tech, practical architecture and almost camouflaged design calls to mind a villain's hidden base. The Residencia was indeed picked to stage the final battle of the 2008 James Bond film Quantum of Solace.
explore: John Colosimo took the photograph and shared it in the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group. ESO regularly reviews that group and picks the best photos for its Picture of the Week series or its gallery.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure landscape photograph of the Paranal Residencia under a starry sky. No camera settings beyond the long exposure are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points, but a long exposure records their slow movement across the sky as trails.

alt: Star trails streaking across a dark sky above the Paranal Residencia.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy Messier 95, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows Messier 95 (M95, or NGC 3351), about 35 million light-years away in the constellation Leo (The Lion). It is a barred spiral galaxy. A bar of stars cuts through its centre and is ringed by an inner ring where new stars are forming.

Pierre Méchain discovered the galaxy in 1781, and Charles Messier catalogued it just four days later. Messier mainly hunted comets and was often annoyed by objects that looked like comets but were not, so he built his catalogue to help others avoid the same confusion.

Messier 95 has also hosted a supernova, the explosive end of a massive star. SN 2012aw appeared in the outer part of one of its spiral arms. Once its light faded, astronomers compared images from before and after the explosion to find which star had vanished. It was a red supergiant up to 26 times as massive as the Sun.
explore: The picture was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 through five filters, from ultraviolet to near-infrared light. Like Messier 95, our own Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy, with a bar of stars running through its centre.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed Messier 95 in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Some of these filters record ultraviolet and near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint for unaided eyes.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a bar through its centre surrounded by an inner ring of star formation.

caption: The blue compact dwarf galaxy ESO 553-46, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Clusters of young, hot stars speckle the small galaxy ESO 553-46 with a fierce blue glow, and the gas around them shines bright red. The stars' intense radiation is what lights up that gas. ESO 553-46 is a dwarf galaxy, yet it forms stars faster than almost any other among the 1000 or so galaxies nearest the Milky Way.

In galaxies, size can mislead. Some of the largest are dormant, while some dwarfs make stars at a furious pace. Because of their low mass and telltale colours, galaxies like this are called blue compact dwarfs (BCDs).

BCDs lack the clear core and structure of larger galaxies such as the Milky Way. They are made of many large star clusters held together by gravity. Astronomers find their chemistry interesting because they contain little dust and few elements heavier than helium. Those conditions closely resemble the early Universe, when the first galaxies were starting to form.
explore: Heavier elements are made inside stars and spread through space by supernova explosions. ESO 553-46 lies about 20 million light-years away, and Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took the picture.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed ESO 553-46 in visible and near-infrared light. Young star clusters appear blue and glowing gas red, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and a small galaxy this far away is far too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A small galaxy speckled with blue clusters of young stars and patches of bright red glowing gas.

caption: ALMA antennas under the Moon, ALMA Operations Support Facility, Chile
story: The Moon shines brightly above the Operations Support Facility (OSF) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) in this photograph, while two 12-metre antenna dishes stand in front. The OSF sits at 2900 metres in the Chilean Andes and is a hub of ALMA activity. It houses staff and contractors and runs all the scientific operations for the array's daily work.

The two antennas were brought down from their observing site for a check-up on special calibration pads. The tests cover computers and motors, and they make sure each dish surface is accurate to within less than a human hair's thickness. They also confirm that a dish can point precisely enough to spot a golf ball 15 kilometres away.
Afterwards the antennas will return to the Chajnantor Plateau, at 5000 metres. Each weighs around 100 tonnes, and two huge custom-built transporters named Otto and Lore will carry them back.
explore: Otto and Lore have a top speed of 12 kilometres per hour. Once back in position on the plateau, the antennas will rejoin the rest of the array and resume their observations. The photograph is credited to A. Duro and ESO.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of ALMA's Operations Support Facility at night with the Moon overhead. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can make the Moon and its surroundings look brighter or more evenly lit than they would to the eye.

alt: Two large dish antennas in the foreground with buildings behind them and a bright Moon in the sky above.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 406, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The spiral arms of NGC 406 are filled mainly with young, massive, bluish stars and crossed by dark lanes of dust. Its yellowish central bulge, home to older stars, is less prominent and almost buried in the disc, as is typical for this kind of spiral. Farther galaxies show through the arms as reddish fuzzy spots.

NGC 406 lies in the southern constellation Tucana (the Toucan), some 65 million light-years away. John Herschel discovered it in 1834. It spans about 60 000 light-years, which is roughly half as wide as the Milky Way, and it closely resembles the well-known Whirlpool Galaxy, Messier 51.
Through a moderate-sized amateur telescope, NGC 406 would look like a faint hazy blob, one of thousands like it across the sky. None of the fine detail in this Hubble picture would be visible.
explore: The picture comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with twenty minutes of exposure through each filter. The frame covers 2.7 by 1.6 arcminutes of sky. The deep image also picks up a significant number of more distant background galaxies.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded NGC 406 through a near-infrared filter (F814W), shown in red, and a blue filter (F435W), shown in blue, with a green channel made from the two.
understand.eye: Through a moderate amateur telescope the galaxy would appear only as a faint hazy blob, and the near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see.

alt: A spiral galaxy with bluish arms crossed by dark dust lanes, a small yellowish centre and reddish fuzzy background galaxies showing through.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J1206, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows the galaxy cluster MACS J1206, which lies about 4 billion light-years away. Clusters like this one are worth studying for several reasons.

A galaxy cluster holds an enormous amount of mass, and its gravity is strong enough to bend the path of light visibly, a little like a magnifying glass. That makes clusters useful tools. They amplify the light of distant galaxies behind them, bringing faraway objects within reach.

The lensed images carry information too. Their exact shapes hold clues about spacetime, about how the Universe expands and about how dark matter is spread through the cluster. MACS J1206 is one of 25 clusters studied in the CLASH programme, short for Cluster Lensing and Supernova survey with Hubble. The project is assembling a large collection of scientific data on lensing clusters for astronomers to use.
explore: Hubble observed the cluster with both the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, through filters spanning visible and near-infrared light. The work is credited to M. Postman and the CLASH Team.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed MACS J1206 in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and a cluster this far away is far too faint for any unaided eye.

alt: A Hubble image of the galaxy cluster MACS J1206.

caption: The galaxy NGC 4993 and a kilonova, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
