story: This picture of the galaxy NGC 4993 was made with VIMOS, an instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile. Just above the galaxy's centre, and slightly to its left, is something never seen before, the aftermath of an explosion caused by two neutron stars merging.

Neutron stars are the extremely dense collapsed cores left behind when massive stars die. When two of them spiral together and merge, the result is a rare event called a kilonova. NGC 4993 itself is not unusual. The event inside it is what makes this image special.

The merger did more than shine in visible light. It also produced gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, and gamma rays. LIGO-Virgo detected the gravitational waves, and Fermi and INTEGRAL detected the gamma rays. The galaxy lies about 130 million light-years from Earth.
explore: VIMOS recorded the galaxy through three filters, one in ultraviolet-blue light, one in red light and one at the edge of the near-infrared. The picture is credited to A.J. Levan and N.R. Tanvir.

understand.summary: The VIMOS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope observed NGC 4993 through U, R and z filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxy and the kilonova are far too faint for the unaided eye, and the telescope gathers far more light than the eye can.

scaleExtra: NGC 4993 is about 130 million light-years from Earth, according to ESO.
alt: A galaxy, with the site of a kilonova just above and slightly left of its centre.

caption: The face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3982, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Pink patches of glowing hydrogen, where stars are forming, line the winding arms of NGC 3982, along with clusters of newborn blue stars and dark lanes of dust. At the bright centre lives an older population of stars, packed ever more tightly toward the middle. We see this spiral galaxy face-on.

The universe holds huge numbers of spiral galaxies, and no two look exactly alike. What sets this one apart is how much star birth is going on in its arms. The dust lanes that block some of the light hold the raw material for future generations of stars.

NGC 3982 lies in the constellation Ursa Major, about 68 million light-years away. It spans about 30,000 light-years, one-third the size of our Milky Way. Hubble built up this colour picture over many years, using three of its cameras, the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3.
explore: The wide range of colours comes from photographing the galaxy in both visible and near-infrared light. The team also used a filter that isolates the glow of hydrogen, which picks out the bright star-forming regions scattered along the spiral arms.

understand.summary: Three Hubble cameras recorded NGC 3982 in visible and near-infrared light, plus a filter for glowing hydrogen. Hydrogen regions appear pink and young clusters blue, but the filter-to-colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the galaxy is far too faint to see without a large telescope.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with a bright centre and winding arms lined with pink star-forming regions, blue star clusters and dark dust lanes.
flags: distance mismatch: packet 70 million, caption 68 million light-years

caption: The lenticular galaxy NGC 4526, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Dark lanes of dust and a bright, diffuse glow make NGC 4526 look like a halo hanging in empty space. The calm appearance is misleading. Among lenticular galaxies, a type that sits somewhere between spirals and ellipticals, NGC 4526 is one of the brightest known.

At its centre is a supermassive black hole with the mass of 450 million Suns. The galaxy has also hosted two known supernovae, one in 1969 and one in 1994. It belongs to the Virgo cluster of galaxies, where observations from the ground have shown that a quarter of the galaxies seem to have fast-spinning discs of gas at their centres.

NGC 4526 has the most impressive of these. Its disc of gas, dust and stars stretches unusually far from the centre, spanning some 7% of the galaxy's whole radius, and it spins at more than 250 kilometres per second. Astronomers used the motion of this disc to work out the mass of the central black hole, a method never before used for that purpose.
explore: The picture was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. Judy Schmidt entered a version of it into the Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition, which invited enthusiasts to search the Hubble archive for images the public had never seen.

understand.summary: Hubble observed NGC 4526 in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Some filters record near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy's dust lanes would not be visible to the unaided eye.

alt: A galaxy with a bright, diffuse glow crossed by dark lanes of dust.

caption: The young star cluster NGC 602, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A star cluster sits within a big nebula of gas and dust in many colours. Dark ridges and peaks surround the cluster, lit on their inner sides, while layers of thin, see-through clouds drape over them. A huge number of distant galaxies show through the gas, along with a few much closer stars that appear large and bright.

This is NGC 602, a young star cluster near the edge of the Small Magellanic Cloud. That satellite galaxy is roughly 200 000 light-years from Earth. Its surroundings closely resemble conditions in the early Universe, with very small amounts of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium.

Dark clouds of dense dust and plenty of ionised gas suggest that stars are still forming here. That makes NGC 602 a valuable place to study star birth under conditions very different from those near the Sun. Webb combined its Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) and Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) to make the picture.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI recorded NGC 602 in near- and mid-infrared light. Blue shows 1.15 to 1.5 micrometres, cyan 2.1, green 2.77, yellow 3.35, orange 3.56 and red 4.8 and 10 micrometres.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours are assigned to separate wavelengths rather than being what anyone would see.

alt: A star cluster inside a many-coloured nebula, surrounded by dark ridges of dust lit on their inner sides and thin drifting clouds, with many distant galaxies and a few bright foreground stars.

caption: The merging galaxy NGC 34, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 34 looks less like a galaxy than a glowing creature from the deep ocean. Its outer region seems almost translucent, pricked with stars and odd wispy tendrils, around a bright centre. The galaxy lies in the constellation Cetus (The Sea Monster), about 270 million light-years away.

Its strange look comes from its history. A few million years ago there were two spiral galaxies heading straight for each other. When they collided, their spiral arms and intricate patterns were permanently disrupted.

The bright centre is a product of that merger, which triggered a burst of new star formation and made the surrounding gas glow. As the two galaxies keep blending into one, NGC 34 will lose any distinct shape and become a peculiar galaxy. Collisions between galaxies are rare in the vastness of space, but they can be common in huge clusters that contain hundreds or even thousands of galaxies.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 34 through five filters, from ultraviolet to near-infrared light, including one that picks up glowing hydrogen. The observations are credited to A. Adamo and colleagues.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 34 in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Some of these filters record light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy's faint outer tendrils would be invisible without Hubble.

alt: A galaxy with a bright centre surrounded by a faint, almost translucent outer region with scattered stars and wispy tendrils.

caption: The Moon rising behind the Extremely Large Telescope, Cerro Armazones
story: A full Moon rises from behind Cerro Armazones in Chile's Atacama Desert, and in front of it stands the steel skeleton of the dome of ESO's Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), lit by moonlight. The scene recalls a famous moment in the film E.T., and ESO released it as a Halloween Picture of the Week.

The ELT is still under construction. Its dome frame already stands 80 metres high. Once finished, the whole structure will weigh 6100 tonnes and will be able to turn a full 360 degrees to observe the night sky.

The photograph was taken from about 20 kilometres away, near the entrance to ESO's Paranal Observatory. The Moon is rarely placed so neatly behind the mountaintop, so the Paranal Photo Club planned the shot carefully. As the Moon orbits Earth every 27.3 days it goes through its phases, and the time and place where it rises also shift.
explore: The phases run from new moon through first quarter and full moon to last quarter. In keeping with the season, ESO compared the structure's weight to about 1 500 000 pumpkins. The photograph is credited to J. Beltrán and ESO.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of the ELT dome framework in front of the rising full Moon, taken from about 20 kilometres away. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can record the moonlit steelwork in more detail than the eye would pick out from 20 kilometres away at night.

alt: A large full Moon rising behind a mountaintop with the steel framework of a telescope dome silhouetted in front of it.

caption: A lunar halo over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: A ring of light circles the Moon above ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) in northern Chile, on one of the rare cloudy nights at Paranal Observatory. The scene mixes natural light with artificial light, which gives it an unearthly feel.

The ring is a lunar halo. It forms when moonlight is bent by millions of tiny ice crystals and water droplets in the atmosphere. Such haloes are fairly common, but they need plenty of light, so the Moon has to sit in a particular position relative to Earth and the Sun to reflect enough light for a fine ring like this.

This halo is made of several coloured bands, and they form the same way a rainbow does. Light of different wavelengths is bent by different amounts, so white light splits into its separate colours and spreads into a spectrum.
explore: The photograph was taken by Juan Carlos Muñoz-Mateos and published by ESO. Its unearthly look comes from natural moonlight mixing with artificial light at Paranal, where cloudy skies like these are rare.

understand.summary: This is a night photograph of a lunar halo above the VLT at Paranal. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure may bring out the halo's coloured bands more clearly than the eye would see them at night.

alt: A ring of light with coloured bands circling the Moon in a cloudy night sky above the Very Large Telescope.

caption: The lenticular galaxy Mrk 820, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Mrk 820 shows hints of spiral structure set inside a round halo of stars. Around it, a scattering of other galaxies covers nearly every type, elliptical and spiral. The bright object at the bottom is not a galaxy but a foreground star called TYC 4386-787-1. Most of the other smears and specks are distant galaxies.

Mrk 820 is a lenticular galaxy, classed as S0 on the Hubble Tuning Fork, a scheme that sorts galaxies by shape. Elliptical galaxies, which look like smooth blobs, sit along the handle, ordered by how stretched they are. The rounder ones sit farthest from the prongs, and the more egg-shaped ones sit near the point where the handle splits.

The two prongs hold the spiral galaxies, one for unbarred spirals and one for barred spirals. Lenticular galaxies like Mrk 820 fall in the transition zone between ellipticals and spirals, right at the fork.
explore: Mrk 820 lies about 300 million light-years away. Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took the picture, and Judy Schmidt entered a version of it in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed Mrk 820 through two filters in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint for unaided eyes.

alt: A lenticular galaxy with faint hints of spiral structure in a round halo of stars, surrounded by many small galaxies, with a bright foreground star at the bottom.

caption: The retired Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory
story: The Milky Way stretches as a bright streak above the dish of the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST) at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert. Part of the Milky Way appears in the sky, and part is reflected in the shiny surface of the dish, so almost all of the Milky Way visible from this spot fits into a single frame.

The SEST is now retired. It was shut down in 2003, and its place was taken by two newer facilities on the Chajnantor plateau, the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment telescope (APEX) and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

In its day, the SEST was the largest submillimetre telescope in the southern hemisphere. It broke new ground in studying some of the coldest regions of the Milky Way, where stars are just starting to form from gas and dust. Some of the huge star-forming regions it helped explain lie within the band of light above it.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek took the photograph. ESO also published an annotated version that labels the many sky objects in the frame, among them the bright stars Sirius and Procyon, the Orion Nebula, the Cone Nebula, airglow, zodiacal light and Comet Lovejoy.

understand.summary: This is a night-sky landscape photograph of the SEST dish at La Silla with the Milky Way above it. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed than it would to a watcher.

alt: A large telescope dish on a mountaintop under the bright band of the Milky Way, which is also reflected in the shiny dish.

caption: The lenticular galaxy NGC 5010, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: With its reddish and yellow centre, NGC 5010 looks a little like an explosion in a Hollywood film. The galaxy is seen from the side, which lets Hubble show the dark, dusty bands left over from its spiral arms.

NGC 5010 is changing. Once a spiral galaxy like our Milky Way, it is turning into an elliptical, an older and less defined type. In this in-between stage, astronomers call it a lenticular galaxy, a type with features of both. It has started to grow a big bulge in its disc as it becomes rounder.

Most of its stars are red and old. Few of the short-lived blue stars that fill younger, star-forming galaxies remain, because much of the dust and gas needed to make new stars has already been used up. Over time, NGC 5010 will become more and more "red and dead", the phrase astronomers use for elliptical galaxies.
explore: NGC 5010 lies around 140 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo (The Virgin). Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the picture in violet and infrared light. The dark bands are what remain of dust once spread along its spiral arms.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded NGC 5010 in violet and infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the galaxy's faint dust bands would not be visible without a large telescope.

alt: A side-on galaxy with a reddish and yellow centre crossed by dark, dusty bands.

caption: The overlapping galaxies NGC 3314a and NGC 3314b, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: At the top left of this picture from ESO's VLT Survey Telescope (VST), two spiral galaxies, NGC 3314a and NGC 3314b, seem to overlap. The two are not interacting at all. They lie at different distances in the constellation Hydra and only line up when seen from Earth.

The chance alignment is useful. It lets astronomers measure a range of the galaxies' properties, including how their dust absorbs starlight, and learn about what they are made of and how they have changed.

At lower right sits a faint yellowish smudge, an ultra-diffuse galaxy (UDG) called UDG 32. UDGs are as large as the Milky Way but have 100 to 1000 times fewer stars. They are very faint and lack gas to form stars. Within the Hydra I cluster, few galaxies are as faint or as spread out as UDG 32. A study led by Enrichetta Iodice suggests it may have formed from filaments reaching out of NGC 3314a, but more observations are needed.
explore: The picture is part of the VST Early-type Galaxy Survey (VEGAS), which studies very faint structures in galaxy clusters. Iodice works at Italy's Istituto Nazionale di Astrofisica. The VST's OmegaCAM camera recorded the field through two visible-light filters.

understand.summary: OmegaCAM on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope recorded this field through g and r filters in visible light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultra-diffuse galaxy is far too faint for the eye to see, and the telescope's exposures gather far more light.

scaleExtra: The two galaxies lie between 117 and 140 million light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: Two overlapping spiral galaxies at top left and a faint yellowish smudge of an ultra-diffuse galaxy at lower right.

caption: The lensed galaxy LRG-3-817, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A long arc curves to the left of a central cluster of galaxies in this Hubble picture. The arc is the galaxy LRG-3-817 (catalogued too as SDSS J090122.37+181432.3), and its image has been stretched by gravitational lensing.

Lensing happens when a large mass, a galaxy cluster for instance, lies between us and a far-off light source. Massive objects warp space, so light from the far object bends on its way to us and arrives as a distorted image. Einstein's general theory of relativity first predicted the effect.

Strong lenses are useful because Hubble can pick out details inside the arcs they create. Lensing also magnifies, bringing into view objects too distant and too dim to detect otherwise. Hubble uses that boost to study objects beyond the reach of its 2.4-metre main mirror, including the most distant galaxies ever seen.
explore: LRG-3-817 was found by the Sloan Bright Arcs Survey, which turned up some of the brightest lensed high-redshift galaxies in the night sky. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded the field through filters from blue-green visible light to the near-infrared.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this field in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Some of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the lensed arc is far too faint for any unaided eye.

alt: A galaxy cluster with a long, curved arc of light to the left of centre.

caption: The Carina Nebula and star clusters above the VLTI Auxiliary Telescopes, Paranal Observatory
story: The Carina Nebula glows intensely red in the middle of this photograph of the sky over ESO's Paranal Observatory. Below it lies the Wishing Well Cluster (NGC 3532). Farther right is the Lambda Centauri Nebula (IC 2944), and above that and slightly left is the Southern Pleiades (IC 2632). In the foreground stand three of the four Auxiliary Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI).

The Carina Nebula lies in the constellation Carina (The Keel), about 7500 light-years away. It is the sky's brightest nebula, home to several of the Milky Way's brightest and most massive known stars, among them Eta Carinae. That makes it an ideal place to study the violent birth and death of massive stars.

The Wishing Well Cluster earned its name because, through an eyepiece, it resembles silver coins glinting at the bottom of a well. The Lambda Centauri Nebula is a cloud of glowing hydrogen and newborn stars.
explore: Some people see a bird in the Lambda Centauri Nebula's brightest part, hence its nickname, the Running Chicken Nebula. Through the VLTI, the Auxiliary Telescopes or the 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes can work as one giant telescope, used to study discs around young stars and active galactic nuclei. ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi took the photograph.

understand.summary: This is a night-sky landscape photograph of Paranal Observatory with several nebulae and star clusters above the telescopes. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure brings out the Carina Nebula's red glow, which the eye sees far more faintly, if at all, in the night sky.

alt: A starry sky with a bright red nebula in the centre and star clusters around it, above three of the VLTI's Auxiliary Telescopes.

caption: The radio galaxy 4C 73.08 and its neighbours, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: In this Hubble frame, galaxies glow like fireflies against the dark. At the centre sits 4C 73.08, a giant elliptical galaxy. A prominent spiral, viewed from above, shines near the bottom, and other galaxies appear edge-on.

In the visible and near-infrared light used here, 4C 73.08 looks calm. At longer wavelengths it changes character. Radio waves, which pass through dust, reveal plumes streaming from its core, where a supermassive black hole shoots out twin jets of material. That radio activity is why it is classed as a radio galaxy.

Astronomers need to study such objects at many wavelengths to learn what they really are, much as a firefly's glow tells a scientist only a little about the insect. Visible light shows a galaxy's structure and the ages of its stars. 4C 73.08 is clearly redder than the bluer spiral, because it holds many older red stars, so it is the older of the two.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took the picture through two filters. One captures green light, and the other captures red and near-infrared light. Radio observations, not shown here, are what reveal the galaxy's jets.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded this field through a green filter and a red and near-infrared filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the radio jets described here do not appear in this picture at all.

alt: A large elliptical galaxy at the centre, a bluer spiral seen face-on below it and several edge-on galaxies around them.

caption: Gravitational lensing around the galaxy cluster SDSS J1110+6459, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright blue crescent stands out at once in this Hubble picture. It is a galaxy, although its odd shape makes that hard to guess. Its image has been bent by gravitational lensing.

The massive galaxy cluster SDSS J1110+6459, which lies to the lower left of the blue streak, is warping the spacetime around it and changing the path of any light passing nearby. A few other signs of lensing are dotted around the same area, including streaks, blobs, curved lines and distorted shapes.

The frame also holds a rare kind of galaxy called a jellyfish galaxy. It sits right next to the cluster and seems to drip bright blue material. Galaxies like this lose gas through ram pressure stripping. As the galaxy moves through space, drag pulls its gas away, leaving trails behind it.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster through four filters, from violet visible light to the near-infrared. Judy Schmidt is acknowledged for the image, which was released as an ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this field in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Some of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and these distant galaxies are far too faint for unaided eyes.

alt: A bright blue crescent-shaped galaxy with a galaxy cluster to its lower left, and next to the cluster a galaxy trailing bright blue material.

caption: The one-armed dwarf galaxy NGC 4625, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A single spiral arm gives the dwarf galaxy NGC 4625 a lopsided look in this Hubble picture. The galaxy lies about 30 million light-years away in the constellation Canes Venatici (The Hunting Dogs). Spiral galaxies normally have at least two arms, and astronomers studied NGC 4625 at several wavelengths to find out why this one has only one.

Ultraviolet observations gave the first clue. In ultraviolet light, the galaxy's disc appears four times larger than it does here. That suggests many very young, hot stars are forming in its outer regions, stars that shine mainly in the ultraviolet. These young stars are around one billion years old, making them roughly 10 times younger than the stars at the visible centre.

Astronomers first thought a nearby dwarf galaxy, NGC 4618, was driving this burst of star formation and had stripped NGC 4625 of all but one arm. In 2004 they found evidence supporting the idea of an interaction between the two.
explore: The 2004 finding was that NGC 4625 has strongly disturbed the gas at the outer edges of NGC 4618. The picture comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and was released as a Picture of the Week.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded NGC 4625 in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet glow that reveals the galaxy's larger disc is invisible to the eye and does not appear in this visible-light picture.

alt: A small galaxy with a bright centre and a single spiral arm curling around one side.
flags: caption's 2004 evidence sentence reverses the two galaxies' roles

caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 4789A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The stars of NGC 4789A are smeared across the sky in a jumble with no clear order, a mix of blue and red. This dwarf irregular galaxy in the constellation Coma Berenices looks far more subtle and abstract than bright spiral or elliptical galaxies. Many more distant galaxies appear as fuzzy shapes around it.

The stars may look randomly scattered, but gravity holds them all together. Their colours have been deliberately exaggerated here to bring out the mix. The blue stars are bright, hot and massive, and they formed fairly recently. The red stars are much older. Finding both means the galaxy has been forming stars throughout its history.

Lying just over 14 million light-years from us, NGC 4789A is relatively close, which lets Hubble pick out many of its individual stars. The name fits well. A dwarf irregular galaxy is small and has no regular shape such as a spiral or an ellipse.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the galaxy through visible and near-infrared filters. Judy Schmidt, also known as Geckzilla, is acknowledged for the image. The fuzzy background shapes are galaxies much farther away than NGC 4789A.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 4789A in visible and near-infrared light. The colours have been deliberately exaggerated to separate blue and red stars, and the exact mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The colours are exaggerated on purpose, so the contrast between blue and red stars is much stronger than any natural view.

alt: A loose, irregular scattering of blue and red stars with fuzzy distant galaxies in the background.

caption: Cold dust clouds in the Carina Nebula, imaged by APEX and the Curtis Schmidt telescope
story: Orange tones trace the cold, dusty clouds of the Carina Nebula, where stars form, laid over a visible-light view of the region. The orange layer comes from the APEX telescope and its LABOCA camera, observing submillimetre light at a wavelength of 870 µm. The visible-light picture was taken with the Curtis Schmidt telescope, which stands at Cerro Tololo Interamerican Observatory.

The Carina Nebula is a site of violent star formation and home to some of the most massive stars in our galaxy. That makes it a good place to study how young stars interact with the molecular clouds they were born from.

The numbers are large. The nebula contains stars adding up to more than 25 000 Suns, and its clouds of gas and dust hold about 140 000 Suns' worth of mass. Cold dust gives off little visible light but glows at submillimetre wavelengths, which is why APEX can map it.
explore: The Carina Nebula lies about 7500 light-years away. The submillimetre data are credited to T. Preibisch and colleagues, and the optical image to N. Smith of the University of Minnesota.

understand.summary: APEX's LABOCA camera recorded cold dust at a submillimetre wavelength of 870 µm, shown in orange, over a visible-light image from the Curtis Schmidt telescope.
understand.eye: Submillimetre light is invisible to the eye, so the orange clouds show cold dust that cannot be seen directly.

alt: A wide view of the Carina Nebula with orange-tinted clouds of cold dust laid over the glowing nebula.

caption: Laser guide stars from a Unit Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: Powerful laser beams shoot out from the dome of a Unit Telescope, one of four that make up ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Chile's Paranal Observatory. The beams climb to a layer of air about 90 kilometres up that is rich in sodium atoms. The lasers make that sodium glow, creating artificial stars.

The reason is Earth's atmosphere, which distorts incoming light and blurs astronomical observations. The same effect makes stars twinkle. To correct for it, astronomers use adaptive optics, in which a flexible mirror changes shape hundreds of times per second to cancel out the turbulence.

Working out those corrections requires a reference star close to the target, and real stars are not always well placed. Lasers let astronomers put an artificial star exactly where it is needed, whenever they need it.
explore: The sodium atoms that the lasers excite are left over from meteoroids that burned up in Earth's atmosphere at the end of their journeys through the Solar System. So the VLT uses material from space to help it observe space. The photograph is credited to M. Zamani and ESO.

understand.summary: This is a night photograph of laser beams from one of the VLT's Unit Telescopes. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can make the laser beams look brighter and more solid than they would to someone standing nearby.

alt: Laser beams shining upward from a telescope dome into the night sky.

caption: The emission nebula NGC 6188, photographed by J. Pérez for ESO
story: The nebula NGC 6188 glows red in this photograph. The colour comes from hydrogen gas, lit up by massive stars that formed recently. The nebula lies in the southern constellation Ara (the Altar), some 4000 light-years away.

NGC 6188 is an emission nebula, a cloud of gas that shines with its own light because nearby hot stars energise it. It sits inside a large, dark molecular cloud. Clouds like that are dense and cold, and they are where new stars are born.

The ultraviolet light of hot young stars is what makes hydrogen in nebulae like this one shine, and the red glow is the typical colour of that hydrogen emission. The photograph is credited to J. Pérez and ESO.

understand.summary: ESO does not name the telescope, camera or filters. The red colour is emission from hydrogen.
understand.eye: The nebula is too faint for the eye to see in colour, and a camera exposure gathers far more light.

scaleExtra: NGC 6188 is some 4000 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: A red-glowing cloud of hydrogen gas set within a dark molecular cloud.

caption: The merged galaxy 2MASX J16270254+4328340, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Long trails of fine mist, made of millions of stars, stream from the galaxy 2MASX J16270254+4328340. It has merged with another galaxy, and the trails are left over from that collision. Despite the apparent chaos, Hubble caught the merger near its end.

The most intense phase came earlier. The two galaxies disturbed each other's gas clouds so badly that the clouds collapsed and set off a burst of star formation. That surge used up almost all of the gas, leaving the galaxy unable to make new stars.

The galaxy is now heading into old age. As things settle, its stars will redden as they age and eventually die off one by one. With no new generations to replace them, the galaxy begins a slow decline. The name, a string of letters and numbers, is simply a catalogue label.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took the picture through a blue filter and a red filter. Judy Schmidt, known as Geckzilla, is acknowledged for the image, which was released as an ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded this galaxy through blue and red filters in visible light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The faint trails of stars would be far too dim to see without Hubble's long exposures.

alt: A galaxy with long, misty trails of stars streaming away from it after a merger.

caption: The pure-disc galaxy NGC 3621, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: NGC 3621 has a flat disc crossed by dark lanes, with spiral arms where young stars form in clusters that show up as blue dots. Its centre simply grows brighter, with no true bulge. Background galaxies and a few bright foreground stars from our own Milky Way also appear.
Most spiral galaxies have a central bulge, a compact, rounded crowd of old stars. NGC 3621 is a pure-disc galaxy and lacks one, unlike NGC 6744, for example.

It is also believed to host an active supermassive black hole that is swallowing matter and giving off radiation. That is somewhat unusual, because such active galactic nuclei are mostly found in galaxies with large bulges. This black hole is thought to be fairly light, around 20 000 times the mass of the Sun, and two smaller black holes of a few thousand solar masses are thought to lie near the nucleus. NGC 3621 may have three black holes at its heart.
explore: The galaxy lies in the constellation Hydra (The Sea Snake), about 22 million light-years away, and a moderate-sized telescope can show it. ESO took this picture with the FORS1 instrument on the VLT through B, V and I filters.

understand.summary: The FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope recorded NGC 3621 through B, V and I filters. Young star clusters appear as blue dots, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: A moderate-sized telescope shows the galaxy, but not the fine detail here, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A spiral galaxy with dark dust lanes and blue star clusters in its arms, a centre that brightens without a bulge, and background galaxies and foreground stars around it.

caption: The irregular galaxy IC 3583, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This delicate blue group of stars is an irregular galaxy called IC 3583, some 30 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo (The Virgin). It seems to have no clear structure, but astronomers have found a bar of stars running through its centre.

A bar is a straight band of stars that crosses a galaxy's centre. Bars like this are common in the Universe. They appear in most spiral galaxies, in many irregular galaxies and in some lenticular galaxies, which sit between spirals and ellipticals.

Two of our closest neighbours, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, also have bars. That hints that they may once have been barred spiral galaxies that were disrupted or pulled apart by the gravity of the Milky Way. The Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies that orbit the Milky Way.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded IC 3583 through visible and near-infrared filters. The picture was released as an ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week. Lenticular galaxies have a central bulge and a disc but no clear spiral arms.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed IC 3583 in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A loose, delicate group of blue stars forming an irregular galaxy.

caption: The galaxy NGC 4388 in the Virgo Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The outer parts of NGC 4388 look smooth and featureless, like an elliptical galaxy. Its centre tells a different story. Dust lanes are held within two symmetric spiral arms that curl out from a glowing core, a clear mark of a spiral galaxy. Bright blue speckles in the arms show where young stars sit.

NGC 4388 is changing, and its mixed appearance reflects that. It lies some 60 million light-years away and belongs to the Virgo Cluster, a massive collection of over 1300 galaxies bound together by gravity. Life in such a crowded, massive cluster has some unwelcome effects on its members, and NGC 4388 is feeling them.
The young blue stars in its arms show that the galaxy has had recent bursts of star formation. The cluster is one reason the constellation Virgo (The Virgin) is so rich in galaxies.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded NGC 4388 through ultraviolet, blue and near-infrared filters. The picture was released as an ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week. Its blend of elliptical and spiral features gives the galaxy a somewhat confused identity.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 4388 in ultraviolet, blue and near-infrared light. Young stars appear blue, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is ultraviolet or near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint for unaided eyes.

alt: A galaxy with a smooth, featureless outer glow and a centre where dusty spiral arms dotted with blue young stars curl out from a bright core.

caption: The nebula Gum 40 (IC 2872), imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: This gas cloud in the constellation Centaurus is part of the large Running Chicken Nebula. Depending on who is looking, it resembles a playful fox, a skulking hyena or the head of a chicken, and some people see the chicken's rear end instead. The VLT Survey Telescope (VST) at ESO's Paranal Observatory captured it.

Fun nicknames are popular with scientists, but they do not help clear communication in a field as international as astronomy. So this nebula also carries two formal names. In 1955 the Australian astronomer Colin Stanley Gum listed 84 emission nebulae in the southern sky, and this one became Gum 40.

Much earlier, in 1888, the Danish astronomer John Louis Emil Dreyer had compiled the New General Catalogue (NGC), an index of 7840 objects that includes galaxies, star clusters and emission nebulae. He later added two Index Catalogues (IC) with another 5386 objects, and in them this nebula is IC 2872.
explore: The NGC is still in use and was last updated in 2019 with 13 957 new objects. As telescopes and instruments improve, astronomers keep finding more deep-sky objects, so these catalogues will never be finished. The image is credited to the VPHAS+ team and ESO.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope at Paranal recorded this nebula. The camera and filters aren't named, and the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The nebula is too faint for the eye to see in this detail, and the telescope's exposures gather far more light.

alt: A glowing gas cloud whose shape some people compare to an animal's head.

caption: ALMA antennas under the night sky, Chajnantor plateau
story: ALMA's antennas stand across the Chajnantor plateau in this panorama, which spans about 180 degrees from north at left to south at right. In front, 12-metre antennas work together as one giant telescope. At far left, a group of smaller 7-metre antennas for ALMA's compact array is lit up. The crescent Moon, out of frame, casts stark shadows over all of them.

The brightest "star" at left is the planet Jupiter. Only the Moon and Venus outshine it among natural objects in the night sky. On the right are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, dwarf irregular galaxies orbiting the Milky Way at about 160 000 and 200 000 light-years. The Large one looks like a puff of smoke above the rightmost antenna.

At far left, the elongated smudge of the Andromeda galaxy appears. It is our closest major neighbouring galaxy and the biggest member of the Local Group, which counts about 30 galaxies including ours.
explore: Andromeda contains approximately one trillion stars, over twice the Milky Way's count, and is the only major galaxy visible without a telescope. Only its central region shows here, though it spans six full Moons on the sky. Babak Tafreshi, founder of The World At Night, took the photograph.

understand.summary: This is a panoramic night-sky photograph of ALMA on the Chajnantor plateau. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so faint objects like the Magellanic Clouds look brighter than a watcher would see them.

alt: A wide panorama of large dish antennas on a plateau at night, with a bright planet at left, two faint cloud-like galaxies at right and a small elongated galaxy at far left.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 3568, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble sees NGC 3568, a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Centaurus, from the side. In 2014, light from a supernova in this galaxy reached Earth. A supernova is the sudden, brilliant flare of light from the explosion that ends a massive star's life.

Most astronomical discoveries come from teams of professional astronomers, but amateurs with New Zealand's Backyard Observatory Supernova Search found this one. Dedicated amateurs often make such finds, especially of short-lived events like supernovae.

This Hubble observation belongs to a large collection of data gathered to prepare for science with the James Webb Space Telescope. Pairing Hubble data with observations from the ground, astronomers have built a rich archive on the links between young stars and the cold gas clouds they form in. Webb observes in infrared light, so it can see through the gas and dust of stellar nurseries to the young stars inside, and it will even let astronomers study faint protostellar cores.
explore: A central aim for Webb is tracing how stars live and die, above all where and how they form. The Hubble data came from two cameras, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys, and the observations are credited to M. Sun.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 3568 in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is ultraviolet or near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint for unaided eyes.

scaleExtra: NGC 3568 lies roughly 57 million light-years from the Milky Way, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: A barred spiral galaxy seen from the side.

caption: A VLTI Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: This ESO picture marks the first light of one of the Auxiliary Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI).

AT4, the fourth and last of the VLTI Auxiliary Telescopes to be installed, achieved first light on the night of 15 December 2006. First light is the moment a new telescope takes its first images of the sky.

Those first images showed that AT4 would be able to match the excellent image quality of the first three Auxiliary Telescopes. It was soon to join them in routine interferometric measurements. In interferometry, light from several telescopes is combined so that together they can see finer detail than any one of them alone. With the fourth telescope in place, the full set of Auxiliary Telescopes would be able to work together.

understand.summary: This ESO picture relates to the first light of the VLTI Auxiliary Telescope AT4. No camera settings or filters are published.
understand.eye: No details of how the picture was made are published, so how it compares with a view by eye is unknown.

alt: A VLTI Auxiliary Telescope at the time of its first light.
flags: subject of image not described in caption

caption: The open star cluster Haffner 18, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Three stages of star formation share this frame. At the centre is Haffner 18, whose mature stars have already cleared away the nebulae they were born in. At the lower left of the cluster sits a very young star still wrapped in its birth cocoon of gas. Toward the right corner, dust clouds are active stellar nurseries that will make more stars in the future.
The one scene covers the past, present and future of star birth. Haffner 18 is an open cluster of about 50 stars, several of them massive and short-lived.

The young massive star with the cryptic name FM3060a still sits inside a small, dense hydrogen shell. That shell measures about 2.5 light-years across and is growing at 20 km/s. It must have formed some 40,000 years ago.
explore: The cluster lies between 25,000 and 30,000 light-years away. The picture was made with the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope through B, V, R and I filters, and it is credited to ESO.

understand.summary: FORS2 on ESO's Very Large Telescope recorded Haffner 18 through B, V, R and I filters in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the telescope gathers far more light than the eye can.

alt: A cluster of mature stars at the centre, a young star wrapped in gas at its lower left and dust clouds toward the right corner.

caption: The galaxy cluster RCS2 J2327, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: The heart of the galaxy cluster RCS2 J2327 sits at the centre of this frame. A diffuse blue and white overlay spread across the picture is a mass map, showing how much mass is thought to lie in each region. The cluster is one of the most massive known at its distance or beyond.

Objects this massive warp the space around them, an effect called gravitational lensing. They bend, distort and magnify the light of more distant objects, bringing into view galaxies that would otherwise be too far away to detect. Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts the effect.

Strong lensing produces distorted galaxies and sweeping arcs, and both appear here. Weak lensing is subtler and hard to see directly. It is mostly studied statistically, but it offers a way to measure the masses of objects in space. Using weak lensing, the study found that RCS2 J2327 contains the mass of two quadrillion Suns.
explore: The picture combines observations from the HAWK-I instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope and Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Combining the two gives a detailed, collaborative way to study weak lensing.

understand.summary: This composite combines Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys data in visible and near-infrared light with HAWK-I infrared data from the VLT, plus a blue and white mass map. The colour mapping of the filters isn't published.
understand.eye: The blue and white mass map is not light at all but a chart of where mass is thought to be, and the infrared data are invisible to the eye.

alt: A galaxy cluster at the centre with distorted galaxies and sweeping arcs, overlaid with a diffuse blue and white haze showing a mass map.

caption: The road to the Very Large Telescope under the Magellanic Clouds, Paranal Observatory
story: A road winds through the desert in the centre of this photograph, linking the VISTA telescope's peak, where the picture was taken, to ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) on Cerro Paranal. Above, two distinct bright patches mark the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, and the path of the Milky Way runs down the left side.

These two neighbouring galaxies of the Milky Way lie about 160 000 and 200 000 light-years off. Astronomers use the VLT to study them, our own galaxy and far more distant galaxies billions of light-years away.

Cerro Paranal sits 120 km south of the town of Antofagasta in Chile's Atacama Desert. Its distance from towns means light pollution is essentially absent, and neither road traffic nor dust from mines disturbs the work there. The desert air also holds very little moisture, which helps keep observing conditions excellent.
explore: Paranal Observatory is home to both the VLT and VISTA, which stands on an adjacent peak. The photograph is credited to José Francisco Salgado and ESO. The Magellanic Clouds are two separate galaxies, the Large and the Small, not clouds in Earth's sky.

understand.summary: This is a night-sky landscape photograph of Paranal taken from the VISTA peak. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way appear brighter than a watcher would see them.

alt: A road winding through a dark desert toward telescopes on a distant peak, with two bright cloud-like patches in the sky and the Milky Way at left.

caption: The spiral galaxy UGC 9391, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The star-studded spiral arms of UGC 9391 stand alone against a backdrop of distant galaxies, which show only as faint swirls and smudges. Some much brighter foreground stars, far closer to us, are ringed with diffraction spikes, caused by light interacting with the inner parts of Hubble's optics.

UGC 9391 lies 130 million light-years away in the constellation Draco, close to the north celestial pole. Hubble observed it as part of work on the Cosmic Distance Ladder, a chain of linked measurements that lets astronomers find distances to the farthest objects.

Distances can be measured directly only for fairly nearby objects, closer than about 3000 light-years. Beyond that, astronomers rely on relationships calibrated against nearby objects. UGC 9391 gave them a natural laboratory for comparing two methods, one using supernova explosions and the other Cepheid variable stars. Sharper distances help measure how fast the Universe is expanding, a key goal for Hubble.
explore: The picture comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from visible to near-infrared light. The observations are credited to A. Riess and colleagues. Cepheid variables are pulsating stars whose brightness rises and falls in a regular rhythm.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed UGC 9391 in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A spiral galaxy with star-studded arms among faint distant galaxies, with bright foreground stars showing diffraction spikes.

caption: An ancient petroglyph beneath the stars, near La Silla Observatory
story: An ancient stone engraving, or petroglyph, sits near ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. Carved on its face are figures of people alongside llamas or similar wild camelids. Behind it, the stars glow faintly over the mountain ridge, and one of La Silla's telescopes stands in silhouette.

Petroglyphs are found across the world, and in some places they date back as far as 40 000 BCE. This one is much more recent. The native nomadic peoples of the Atacama Desert once followed herds of camelids across the dry, harsh land. Later they settled, creating desert oases where they bred the animals.
In the photograph, that ancient carving shares the frame with the silhouette of a modern observatory built for exploring space, setting prehistory and the present side by side.
explore: The photograph is credited to H. Dahle and ESO. This petroglyph is much younger than the oldest known examples, although no age is given for it. Llamas belong to the camelid family, which also includes camels.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph of a petroglyph near La Silla with a telescope and stars behind. No camera settings are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can gather more starlight than the eye, so the sky may look brighter than it would to someone standing there.

alt: An engraved stone showing figures of people and llamas in the foreground, with faint stars above a mountain ridge and a telescope silhouetted behind.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory
story: Stars swirl in long trails around the sky's south pole above ESO's La Silla Observatory. The picture combines a long series of separate images, so Earth's rotation shows up as the stars' circling paths.

The MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's silver dome stands in the foreground. Behind it are the ESO 1-metre Schmidt telescope in its white dome and the boxy New Technology Telescope building, and at the back the ESO 3.6-metre telescope's double domes sit beside a smaller neighbour, the now-retired Coudé Auxiliary Telescope.

Three horizontal streaks cross the sky from left to right. They do not turn with the stars, which shows they are much closer to home. They are aeroplanes. The observatory sits close to a fairly busy flight path, and these trails come from aircraft flying from Calama to Santiago.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Alexandre Santerne took the photograph. When he is not photographing observatories, he travels the world, Chile included, for his research on planets orbiting other stars. Stars appear to circle the sky's poles because Earth spins on its axis.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape made by combining many exposures at La Silla, which turns stars into trails. No other camera settings are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, but combining many exposures records their slow circling as long trails.

alt: Long star trails curving around the sky's south pole above several telescope domes and buildings, with three straight horizontal streaks from aircraft crossing the sky.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4455, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Scattered points of light like sequins make up NGC 4455, a spiral galaxy in the northern constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair). The galaxy is about 45 million light-years away, and Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took the picture.

The constellation's name is unusual. Coma Berenices is the only modern constellation named in honour of a real historical person, Queen Berenice II of Egypt. She ruled the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, in what is now Libya, and later became queen of Ptolemaic Egypt after marrying her cousin, Ptolemy III Euergetes.

She became known for offering locks of her hair so that her husband would come home safely from battle. He did return, but the hair, left in a Zephyrium temple, vanished. The story goes that it had been stolen and set among the stars. If the hair did land in NGC 4455, it made quite a journey.
explore: The observations are credited to I. Karachentsev and colleagues. Coma Berenices means Berenice's Hair, a name drawn from the story of the queen's offering of her locks. The galaxy's scattered points of light earned it the comparison to sequins.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded NGC 4455. The filters aren't listed, and the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope, and Hubble gathers far more light than the eye can.

alt: A spiral galaxy made of scattered points of light like sequins.
